title_original: Cheyco Leidmann: the Red That Bleeds, the Gold That Burns

blocks.text: He was six years old. He was handed a Bolex 8mm camera, complete with its full editing kit, the way other children are given a ball or a bicycle. “I was immediately fascinated by moving images, and by the manipulation of those images through editing,” Cheyco Leidmann recalls. He cites Orson Welles and Touch of Evil , a film that “branded him.” Listening to him, it becomes clear that everything starts there: in the early conviction that an image never really tells the truth.

Cheyco Leidmann has never presented himself as a photographer. “These aren’t photos,” he was already correcting people in 1998. “Anyone can be a photographer these days, even with a phone. No, these are images. They’re worked.” It has to be understood this way: no Photoshop, no editing, everything shot on slide film, everything done in the camera. A red, ketchup-colored ice cream, a California license plate reading “FOXY LADY,” a green latex-gloved hand gripping a Cadillac hood. For him, genuine artistic value is the product of meticulous, almost surgical work, the point where glamour, provocation and art collide.

There is something of Nadar in this way of building a myth before the work itself, something of Kerouac in the American road he never stopped traveling, Downtown LA, Soda Lake, Fort Lauderdale, and a touch of Buñuel in these bodies that emerge from cars like surrealist apparitions. He himself prefers to cite Hunter S. Thompson. “One of my favorite books is Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas ,” he confides. Reading him, it is no longer surprising that his world resembles a hallucinated road trip in which advertising has seized power.

Foxy Lady was published right in the fertile years of the 1980s and became an instant cult object, sold out, reissued, copied to the point of exhaustion. “My style got copied, admired, criticized and, worse still, my images were stolen,” he said of his 2018 collaboration with stylist Adam Selman. “These are individuals who use other people’s ideas because they are too poor to create something of their own.” The line lands hard.

His longtime creative partner is Ypsitylla von Nazareth, stylist and muse, present since Foxy Lady through his most recent campaigns. “She has taken charge of every production process that followed, right up to today,” he says of her, with the same economy of words he reserves for what truly matters.

From California light, Leidmann shifted one day toward darker visions, the series Toxytt, its fragments, its frontal violence. The shift is surprising, given how opposed the two worlds seem, yet he speaks of it with the same quiet nonchalance. Asked about any regrets, he first deflects, “I am completely low tech,” before delivering the line that sums up his entire system: “I do not try to find out what technique you use to eat.” People inevitably read provocation into it. He defends himself with the same economy of words: “Provoking for the sake of provoking is like buying a ticket to your own concert: it is pointless. It is simply what I feel.”

Then there is the question of the gesture itself, of what happens in the instant of the shutter click. On the secret of the perfect frame: “The eyes are the weapon. You have to think subversively. It all comes down to speed, experience, discipline, reaction, precision and luck, all coming together in a moment of nihilistic silence,” he told Dazed . A few words later, he adds that under these conditions, nine shots out of ten come out right. He is to be believed.

Art? He calls the word “unpleasant, inflationary, a sticker, a price tag, a tool of manipulation.” Cheyco Leidmann thinks as he pleases, lives as he pleases, wherever he pleases, Paris, New York, Miami, Los Angeles, never settling anywhere. “I consider myself a restless, cosmopolitan man,” he says, “I live where I like to live, in Toxytt City,” a city of his own invention, entirely fabricated yet entirely believable, much like his photographs. At YellowKorner, the series “Foxy Lady” and “Silicon” hold the two ends of this America: chrome-plated California on one side, humid Florida on the other. The colors have not shifted a shade.
